title: Responsible AI, Fairness, and Governance
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Responsible AI, Fairness, and Governance ##### The credit model that had never seen a woman approved A non-banking financial company in Chennai built a loan-approval model in 2024. Gradient-boosted trees, 91% AUC on holdout, clean cross-validation, MLflow-tracked, deployed behind a FastAPI service. By every metric on Day 21's rigorous-evaluation checklist, it was a good model. Nine months in, a compliance officer ran a routine slice report and found that the approval rate for women applicants was 11.4%. For men it was 34.8%. Gender was not a feature. Nobody had put it in. But the model had `occupation_category`, `years_at_current_employer`, `mobile_number_registered_to_applicant`, and `co_applicant_present` — and in the historical training data, which spanned 2019 to 2023, women applicants disproportionately had employment gaps, phones registered to a spouse, and a male co-applicant listed first. The model learned those correlates perfectly, because that is what models do. Worse: the *labels* were poisoned too. The training target was "did a loan officer approve this application." Loan officers in 2019–2021 had approved women at a lower rate. The model had not discovered a risk signal. It had learned to imitate a historical human bias with 91% fidelity, and then applied it at 40,000 applications a month with no loan officer in the loop to occasionally make an exception. That is what an unfair model looks like from the inside. It is not a bug you can find in a unit test. It is a model doing exactly what it was trained to do. ##### Where bias actually enters Bias is not one thing. It enters at identifiable points, and knowing the taxonomy tells you where to look. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Historical bias
The world itself is unequal;
the data records it faithfully"] --> E["Model"] B["Representation bias
Some groups under-sampled;
model has little signal for them"] --> E C["Measurement bias
Proxy label ≠ true target
e.g. 'arrested' ≠ 'committed crime'"] --> E D["Aggregation bias
One model for groups that
need different models"] --> E E --> F["Evaluation bias
Benchmark doesn't reflect
deployment population"] F --> G["Deployment bias
Used differently than intended;
feedback loops amplify"] G -.new training data.-> A ``` The Chennai model had four of the six. Historical bias in the officer decisions. Measurement bias, because "approved" was a proxy for "creditworthy." Representation bias, because women were 19% of the training rows. And a feedback loop — rejected applicants never generate repayment data, so the next retrain saw even fewer women who had successfully repaid. That feedback loop is the one that makes fairness problems compound instead of self-correcting. A model that under-approves a group generates less positive data for that group, which makes the next model under-approve them more. ##### Fairness metrics: pick one, and know why There is no single definition of fairness. There are several, they are mathematically incompatible, and choosing among them is an ethical and legal decision, not a statistical one. Let $A$ be the sensitive attribute, $\hat{Y}$ the prediction, $Y$ the true outcome. **Demographic parity (statistical parity).** Selection rate is equal across groups: $P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=a)$ is the same for all $a$. Chennai's model gave 11.4% vs 34.8% — a ratio of 0.33, far below the 0.8 "four-fifths rule" that US employment law uses as a rough screen. Demographic parity ignores $Y$ entirely, which is its strength (it does not trust possibly-biased labels) and its weakness (if base rates genuinely differ, enforcing it costs accuracy). **Equalized odds** (Hardt, Price & Srebro, 2016). True positive rate *and* false positive rate are equal across groups: $P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid Y=y, A=a)$ is the same for all $a$, for $y \in \{0,1\}$. This says: among people who would actually repay, approve them at the same rate regardless of group; among those who would default, reject at the same rate. It conditions on the truth, so it does not force equal outcomes when base rates differ. **Equal opportunity** is the relaxation that only requires equal TPR. Often the right choice when the harm is denial of a benefit — a qualified applicant being rejected. **Predictive parity.** Precision is equal across groups: given the model said yes, the probability of actually being good is the same. Risk-scoring vendors typically argue for this one. **The impossibility result**: if base rates genuinely differ between groups and your classifier is not perfect, you cannot satisfy equalized odds and predictive parity simultaneously. This is the mathematical core of the 2016 COMPAS dispute — ProPublica measured error-rate balance, Northpointe measured calibration, both were correct, and the metrics could not both hold. **You must choose, and you must be able to defend the choice.** | Metric | Equalises | Choose when | |---|---|---| | Demographic parity | Selection rate | Labels are untrustworthy; legal requirement for representation | | Equal opportunity | TPR | Denying a benefit to a qualified person is the main harm | | Equalized odds | TPR and FPR | Both false denials and false grants cause harm | | Predictive parity | Precision | Downstream users treat the score as a probability | | Calibration by group | Score reliability | Score is consumed by humans as a risk estimate | ##### Measuring it with Fairlearn ```python import pandas as pd from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from fairlearn.metrics import ( MetricFrame, selection_rate, demographic_parity_ratio, equalized_odds_difference, true_positive_rate, false_positive_rate, ) from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score df = pd.read_parquet("data/loan_applications.parquet") sensitive = df["gender"] # kept OUT of features, used for audit X = df.drop(columns=["approved", "gender", "applicant_id"]) y = df["approved"] X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te, s_tr, s_te = train_test_split( X, y, sensitive, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=42 ) model = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=400, random_state=42).fit(X_tr, y_tr) y_pred = model.predict(X_te) mf = MetricFrame( metrics={ "accuracy": accuracy_score, "precision": precision_score, "recall (TPR)": recall_score, "FPR": false_positive_rate, "selection rate": selection_rate, "count": lambda yt, yp: len(yt), }, y_true=y_te, y_pred=y_pred, sensitive_features=s_te, ) print(mf.by_group) print("\nDemographic parity ratio:", round(demographic_parity_ratio( y_te, y_pred, sensitive_features=s_te), 3)) print("Equalized odds difference:", round(equalized_odds_difference( y_te, y_pred, sensitive_features=s_te), 3)) ``` Two things to notice. **The sensitive attribute is excluded from the features but retained for the audit.** "Fairness through unawareness" — just dropping the column — does not work, as Chennai proved; you need the attribute precisely so you can measure whether proxies reconstructed it. And `count` is in the metric set, because a fairness gap computed on 43 test rows is noise, not evidence. ##### Mitigation: three places to intervene **Pre-processing** — change the data before training. Reweighting samples so groups have equal influence, resampling under-represented groups, or learning representations that are statistically independent of $A$. Advantage: model-agnostic. Disadvantage: you are modifying data, which raises its own provenance questions. **In-processing** — change the training objective. Fairlearn's `ExponentiatedGradient` wraps any scikit-learn estimator and solves a constrained optimisation: maximise accuracy subject to a fairness constraint. ```python from fairlearn.reductions import ExponentiatedGradient, EqualizedOdds mitigated = ExponentiatedGradient( estimator=HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=400, random_state=42), constraints=EqualizedOdds(difference_bound=0.03), ) mitigated.fit(X_tr, y_tr, sensitive_features=s_tr) y_fair = mitigated.predict(X_te) ``` Typically the strongest results, but it needs access to training and produces a randomised ensemble that is harder to explain. **Post-processing** — change the decision threshold per group. Hardt et al.'s method finds group-specific thresholds that equalise TPR/FPR. ```python from fairlearn.postprocessing import ThresholdOptimizer post = ThresholdOptimizer( estimator=model, constraints="equalized_odds", objective="accuracy_score", prefit=True, predict_method="predict_proba", ) post.fit(X_tr, y_tr, sensitive_features=s_tr) y_post = post.predict(X_te, sensitive_features=s_te) ``` Simplest and cheapest — you keep your existing model. But it **requires the sensitive attribute at inference time**, and in many jurisdictions applying a different threshold by protected class is itself legally fraught. That tension is real and you should surface it to legal counsel rather than resolve it in a notebook. Always plot the trade-off. Accuracy versus fairness is a frontier, not a single point, and the honest deliverable is the frontier plus a recommended point with reasoning. ##### Privacy: PII, anonymization, differential privacy Fairness and privacy travel together because both are about what your data reveals about people. **PII** is any data identifying an individual: name, phone, Aadhaar, PAN, email, precise location, device ID. Under India's **DPDP Act 2023**, processing personal data requires a lawful basis (usually consent, obtained through clear notice), and Data Principals have rights to access, correction, and erasure. A Data Fiduciary must delete personal data once the purpose is served. Practically, for a data scientist: know which columns are personal, keep them in a restricted store, and be able to actually honour a deletion request — which means knowing which trained models were fit on that person's row. **Anonymization is harder than it looks.** Latanya Sweeney showed that 87% of Americans are uniquely identified by ZIP + birthdate + sex. Netflix's anonymised ratings were de-anonymised against public IMDb reviews. Removing names is *pseudonymisation*, not anonymisation, and pseudonymised data is still personal data under most regimes. Techniques, in ascending strength: - **Masking / tokenisation** — replace the value with a surrogate. Reversible if you keep the map, which means the map is now the crown jewel. - **Generalisation** — pincode 411004 → district Pune; exact age → 30–39 band. - **k-anonymity** — every record indistinguishable from at least k−1 others on quasi-identifiers. Vulnerable to homogeneity attacks; extended by l-diversity and t-closeness. - **Differential privacy** — the only formal guarantee. Add calibrated noise so that the output distribution is nearly identical whether or not any single individual is in the dataset. Formally, a mechanism $M$ is $\varepsilon$-differentially private if for neighbouring datasets $D, D'$ differing in one record, $P(M(D) \in S) \le e^{\varepsilon} P(M(D') \in S)$. $\varepsilon$ is the privacy budget: smaller is more private and noisier. Real deployments use roughly 0.1–10 depending on sensitivity. The budget *composes* — every query spends some, and once it is gone you must stop. ```python import numpy as np def dp_mean(values, lower, upper, epsilon, rng=np.random.default_rng(0)): """Laplace mechanism for a bounded mean.""" clipped = np.clip(values, lower, upper) n = len(clipped) sensitivity = (upper - lower) / n # max change from one record noise = rng.laplace(loc=0.0, scale=sensitivity / epsilon) return float(clipped.mean() + noise) incomes = np.random.default_rng(1).gamma(shape=3, scale=180_000, size=5_000) print("true mean: ₹", round(incomes.mean())) print("dp mean: ₹", round(dp_mean(incomes, 0, 5_000_000, epsilon=0.5))) ``` For ML specifically, DP-SGD (clip per-example gradients, add Gaussian noise) is implemented in Opacus and TensorFlow Privacy. Expect an accuracy cost, and expect it to fall hardest on under-represented groups — DP and fairness can pull against each other, which is exactly the kind of trade-off a governance process exists to adjudicate. ##### Governance: making it institutional Individual conscientiousness does not scale. Governance is the set of mechanisms that make responsible practice the default. **Model cards** (Mitchell et al., 2019) are the core artifact — a one-to-three page document shipped with every model: - **Intended use** and, explicitly, out-of-scope uses - **Training data**: source, period, size, known gaps - **Performance**: overall *and disaggregated by group* - **Fairness assessment**: metrics chosen, why, results, mitigation applied - **Limitations and ethical considerations** - **Owner, version, review date** Write it before deployment, not after an incident. The act of filling in "performance by group" is what forces you to compute it. **Regulation you should know:** - **GDPR** (EU) — lawful basis, data minimisation, right to erasure, and Article 22's right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, plus a right to meaningful information about the logic involved. - **EU AI Act** — risk-tiered. Unacceptable-risk uses banned; **high-risk** (credit scoring, employment, education access, essential services) requires risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, human oversight, and conformity assessment. Obligations phase in through 2026–2027. A loan model like Chennai's is squarely high-risk. - **DPDP Act 2023** (India) — consent and notice, purpose limitation, erasure, Significant Data Fiduciary obligations including audits and impact assessments. - **RBI** guidance on digital lending — transparency on the lending entity, no dark patterns, and grievance redressal, all of which imply your model's decisions must be explainable to a customer. **The operational loop:** an intake review before a project starts (is this an appropriate use of ML at all?), a fairness assessment before deployment, disaggregated monitoring in production wired into Day 38's drift dashboards, an incident process, and a scheduled re-review. Slice metrics by protected group in production, not just at training time — drift is not group-neutral. ##### Common mistakes - **Fairness through unawareness** — dropping the sensitive attribute and assuming the problem is gone. Proxies rebuild it. - Optimising a fairness metric without deciding *which* one is right for the harm at hand. - Reporting fairness gaps without confidence intervals or group sample sizes. - Auditing once at launch and never again. - Treating the label as ground truth when it is a record of past human decisions. - Confusing pseudonymisation with anonymisation. - Spending the differential privacy budget without tracking composition across queries. - Writing the model card after the incident review. - Assuming "we're in India so GDPR doesn't apply" — it applies to EU residents' data wherever you sit, and DPDP imposes parallel duties. - Framing fairness as a purely technical problem. The decision about which metric to enforce belongs to legal, product, and affected communities, not solely to you. ##### Hands-on: audit something real The practical task is the core loop: take a classifier trained on data with a sensitive attribute, compute fairness metrics across groups with `MetricFrame`, apply one mitigation — threshold adjustment is the fastest — and compare the fairness/accuracy trade-off. Plot both points. The gap you give up in accuracy is usually smaller than people fear, and being able to say "we accepted a 0.9-point accuracy reduction to cut the equalized-odds difference from 0.21 to 0.03" is the sentence a risk committee wants to hear. The mini project is a full audit: analyse the data for bias, evaluate multiple fairness metrics, compare two mitigation strategies, and write the model card. Use the UCI Adult income dataset or a German Credit variant if you need public data. The model card is the hardest and most valuable part — write it for a reader who has to decide whether to approve deployment. For the assignment, pick a documented real case: COMPAS recidivism scoring, the Amazon résumé screener that penalised the word "women's," or Apple Card's reported credit-limit disparities. Trace precisely where bias entered using the taxonomy above, name the fairness metric that would have caught it, and describe the governance step — intake review, disaggregated monitoring, model card — that would have surfaced it before harm. ##### Key takeaways - **Bias enters at six identifiable points** — historical, representation, measurement, aggregation, evaluation, deployment — and the fix depends entirely on which one you have. - **Fairness definitions are mutually incompatible**; you must choose one to match the harm, and defend that choice explicitly rather than optimise whatever your library defaults to. - **Removing the sensitive attribute does not remove bias.** Keep it out of the features, keep it available for the audit, and check for proxies. - **Privacy needs formal guarantees**, not just deleted name columns — understand k-anonymity's limits and differential privacy's budget, and know your DPDP/GDPR obligations. - **Governance is what makes it stick**: model cards, disaggregated production monitoring, review gates, and a named owner turn good intentions into a system that catches the next Chennai model before it ships.
